(p-280) The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿And those who are, for their trusts and their pledges, shepherds (guardians)﴾ ﴿And those who are, over their prayers, keep watch﴾ ﴿Those are the inheritors﴾ ﴿who will inherit the Firdaws (Paradise); therein they will abide forever﴾

The majority of readers recited "li-amanatihim" (for their trusts) in the plural, while Ibn Kathir recited "li-amanatihi" (for their trust) in the singular. The trust (amanah) and the covenant ('ahd) together comprise everything a person has taken upon himself of the matters of his religion and his worldly life, in speech and in action. This includes dealings with people, promises, and other things. Observing these means guarding them and fulfilling them. The trust is more general than the covenant, since every covenant is a trust regarding what has been previously committed to in speech, action, or belief, and a trust may arise in matters in which no prior commitment was made. This applies when we take the two in relation to the servant. If we take them in themselves, as God's covenant with His servants and His trust which He entrusted to them, they are at the same level.

The majority recited "ʿalā ṣalawatihim" (over their prayers), while Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "ṣalatihim" (their prayer) in the singular. This singular is a noun of genus and so carries the meaning of the plural. Guarding (muhafaza) the prayer means watching its times closely and hastening to the time of its excellence. "Al-warithun" (the inheritors) refers to Paradise. It is related in the hadith of Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Allah, exalted is He, has made for every person a dwelling in Paradise and a dwelling in the Fire. As for the believers, they take their dwellings and inherit the dwellings of the disbelievers, while the disbelievers take up their dwellings in the Fire."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is possible that Allah, exalted is He, calls attaining Paradise an inheritance because they attained it to the exclusion of others, so it is a metaphorical term in both respects. "Al-Firdaws" is the city of Paradise, and it is the garden of grapevines. The word, according to Mujahid, is Byzantine (Rumi) and was Arabized; it is also said to be Persian and was Arabized. The Arabs call vineyards "faradis." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to the mother of Harithah: "Indeed, it contains many gardens, and your son has attained al-Firdaws."

This hadith in its entirety is in the Musnad of Ibn Abī Shayba.

By Ibn ʿAbbās's saying, "The son of Ādam was created from seven," he meant this verse. By his saying, "His sustenance was placed in seven," he meant His words, Exalted is He: ﴿then We caused grain to grow therein﴾ (ʿAbasa 80:27), ﴿and grapes and herbage﴾ (80:28), ﴿and olives and palm trees﴾ (80:29), ﴿and enclosed gardens of dense trees﴾ (80:30), ﴿and fruit and grass﴾ (80:31), and the verse. Seven of these are for the son of Ādam, and the *abb* (grass) is for livestock. The *qaḍb* (fresh fodder) is eaten by the son of Ādam, and women grow fat on it. This is one view. It was also said: the *qaḍb* is vegetables, because they are cut (*tuqḍab*), so they are the sustenance of the son of Ādam. It was also said: the *qaḍb* and the *abb* are for livestock, and the remaining six are for the son of Ādam, and the seventh is livestock, since they are among the greatest of the son of Ādam's sustenance.

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿Then after that, you will surely die﴾ ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection you will surely be raised﴾ ﴿And We have created above you seven paths, and We were never unaware of creation﴾ ﴿And We sent down water from the sky in measure, then We caused it to settle in the earth, and indeed We are able to take it away﴾ ﴿Then We produced for you by it gardens of date palms and grapevines; in them you have much fruit, and from them you eat﴾ ﴿And a tree that springs forth from Mount Sinai, growing with oil and a condiment for those who eat﴾

"Dhalika" refers to what has been mentioned of these states. Ibn Abi Ablah recited "lama'itun" (with an alif). "Tub'athun" means: you will be raised alive from your graves, and this is a report of resurrection and rising. "Al-tara'iq" (the paths) is everything that is in layers, one above another; from it comes "tarraqtu na'li" (I made layers in my sandal). By "the seven paths" he means the heavens. It is also possible that "al-tara'iq" means "the spread-out things," from "taraqtu al-shay'" (I spread out the thing). His words, exalted is He, ﴿and We were never unaware of creation﴾ are a general negation, meaning: [We were never unaware] of the perfection of their creation, of their interests, and of their deeds.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿in measure﴾: some scholars said it means rain, and some said it means the four rivers: Sayhan, Jayhan, the Euphrates and the Nile.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The correct view is that all of this falls under the water which God, exalted is He, sent down.

Mujahid said: there is no water on the earth except that it comes from the sky.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This may be restricted to sweet water; otherwise, brackish water exists in the earth even during drought, while sweet water becomes scarce in drought. Also, the reports indicate water that existed before the creation of the heavens and the earth. Without doubt, God, exalted is He, has placed water in the earth and sent down water from the sky.

His words, exalted is He, "in measure," meaning: in a beneficial quantity, because if it were abundant, it would destroy.

"Fa-ansha'na" means: We brought into existence and created. God, exalted is He, mentioned "the date palms and the grapevines" because they are the fruit of the Hijaz, in Ta'if, Medina and elsewhere, as al-Tabari said, and because they are also the noblest of fruits. So He mentioned them as an example, not to honour them specially, and as a reminder of them.

His words, exalted is He, "for you in them": it is possible that the pronoun returns to "the gardens," and then it means all kinds of fruit. It is also possible that it returns to "the date palms and the grapevines" specifically, since in them there are grades and varieties. The first is more general, covering all the fruits.

His words, exalted is He, "and a tree": this is conjoined to "gardens," and by it he means the olive tree, which is abundant in Mount Sinai in the land of al-Sham (Syria). It is the mountain on which God, exalted is He, spoke to Moses, peace be upon him, as Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said, along with others. "Al-tur" means the mountain in the speech of the Arabs; it was said that it is one of the words Arabicized from non-Arabic speech. Scholars differed about "Sina'". Qatada said its meaning is "the good," and on this interpretation "al-tur" would have to be read with nunation. Mujahid said its meaning is "blessed." Mu'mar, quoting a group, said its meaning is "possessing trees."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

They would also be obliged to read "al-tur" with nunation. The majority said: it is the name of the mountain, as you say "Jabal Uhud," and "Sina'" is a name, with the mountain added to it.

Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir recited "Sina'" with a kasra on the sin. The rest, and 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, recited "Sayna'" with a fatha on the sin. All of them recited it with a long vowel. On the fatha of the sin, the name is not inflected in any way. On the kasra of the sin, the hamza is like the hamza in "hirba'" (a kind of lizard), and it is not declined in this verse because it has been made the name of a place or a land.

The majority recited "tanbutu" with a fatha on the ta' and a damma on the ba', so the implied sense is: it grows with the oil in it, as you say "Zayd went out with his weapon." Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited "tunbitu" with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the ba'. Scholars differed about the grammatical interpretation of this reading. One group said the ba' is redundant, as in His words, exalted is He, ﴿and do not cast yourselves by your own hands into destruction﴾ [al-Baqara: 195]. In my view this example is open to objection, although Abu 'Ali had cited it, and like the words of the poet:

"We are the sons of Ja'da, lords of the falaj;
we strike with the white swords and hope for relief."

And similar to this. Another group said the implied sense is: it grows its fruit and with it is the oil, so the object is omitted. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi also said this. It has also been said that "nabata" and "anbata" have the same meaning, so the verb would be as in the majority's reading. Al-Asma'i denied "anbata" and accused the poem of Zuhayr in which it appears:

"............. ∗∗∗ ...... anbata al-baql" (the herbage made grow)

Al-Zuhri, al-Hasan and al-A'raj recited "tanbutu" with a damma on the ta' and a fatha on the ba'. Abu al-Fath said the ba' is the ba' of circumstance, meaning: it grows with its oil. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him, it is "takhruju bi-al-duhni," where the ba' is also the ba' of circumstance. Zirr ibn Hubaysh recited "tunbitu" with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the ba', and "al-duhna" with the ba' removed and in the accusative. Sulayman ibn 'Abd al-Malik and al-Ashhab recited "bi-al-dihan."

The purpose in this verse is to enumerate the blessing of olive oil for humankind; it is among the pillars of blessings, without which health cannot do without it. The meaning of the olive tree includes all olive trees, of all their varieties according to the regions.

One group recited "wa-sibghin" (and a condiment). Another group recited "wa-asbagh" (and condiments) in the plural. 'Amir ibn 'Abd Qays recited "wa-mata'an li-al-akilin" (and a provision for those who eat).

"Tub'athun" means: you will be raised alive from your graves, and this is a report of resurrection and rising. "Al-tara'iq" (the paths) is everything that is in layers, one above another; from it comes "tarraqtu na'li" (I made layers in my sandal). By "the seven paths" he means the heavens. It is also possible that "al-tara'iq" means "the spread-out things," from "taraqtu al-shay'" (I spread out the thing). His words, exalted is He, ﴿and We were never unaware of creation﴾ are a general negation, meaning: [We were never unaware] of the perfection of their creation, of their interests, and of their deeds.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿in measure﴾: some scholars said it means rain, and some said it means the four rivers: Sayhan, Jayhan, the Euphrates and the Nile.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The correct view is that all of this falls under the water which God, exalted is He, sent down.

Mujahid said: there is no water on the earth except that it comes from the sky.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This may be restricted to sweet water; otherwise, brackish water exists in the earth even during drought, while sweet water becomes scarce in drought. Also, the reports indicate water that existed before the creation of the heavens and the earth. Without doubt, God, exalted is He, has placed water in the earth and sent down water from the sky.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 23, verses 21–22:

The Exalted and Majestic said:

﴿And indeed, in the cattle there is a lesson for you. We give you to drink from what is in their bellies, and for you in them are many benefits, and from them you eat﴾ ﴿And upon them, and upon the ships, you are carried﴾

"Al-An'am" (the cattle) are camels, cows, sheep and goats, and "al-'ibrah" (the lesson) lies in their creation and in all their conditions.

The majority of readers recited "nusqikum" with a dammah on the nun, from "asqa" (to give to drink), and this is also reported from 'Asim. Nafi', 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir recited "naskikum" with a fathah on the nun, from "saqa." Some people said: "They are two dialects with the same meaning." Others said: "Saqaytuhu" means I gave him water to drink, and "asqaytuhu" means I made for him a share of water for land, a fruit or the like. So it is as if God made the cattle a provision of water for His servants, from which they drink and to which they resort. Abu Ja'far recited "tasqikum" with a ta' on top, meaning: the cattle give you to drink.

"Al-manafi'" (the benefits) are being ridden upon, their hides, their wool, their fleece, and other things too many to count.

"Al-fulk" (the ships) are boats; its singular is "falak." The vowels in the singular are like those in "qafal" and "baradd," and the vowels in the plural are like those in "usud" and "kutub."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 23, verses 23–26:

His the Exalted and Majestic's saying:

﴿Indeed, We sent Noah to his people, and he said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. Will you not then fear Him?"﴾ ﴿So the eminent ones of his people who disbelieved said, "This is not but a man like yourselves who wants to gain superiority over you. And if Allah had willed, He would have sent down angels. We have not heard of this among our forefathers of old."﴾ ﴿He is not but a man in whom there is madness, so wait for him for a time.﴾ ﴿[Noah] said, "My Lord, support me, for they have denied me."﴾

This is the beginning of an illustration for the disbelievers of Quraysh, by means of nations that disbelieved in their prophets and were destroyed. Within this is a warning that a calamity similar to what befell those [nations] may descend upon them.

Noah (peace be upon him) was the first prophet sent to mankind, and Idris (peace be upon him) was the first to be given prophethood but not sent (as a messenger).

And "al-mala'" (the eminent ones): the nobles, because the "mala'" originates from them; it is the plural of "qawm" (people). In their saying "these" there is an expression of disbelief in the sending of a human being, while they were a people who acknowledged the angels. That was, without doubt, firmly established among them from the remnants of the prophethood of Adam, Idris and others (peace be upon them), though it was not based on sound knowledge or acquaintance with the reports of prophethood.

And "al-jinnah": madness. "Tarabbasu" means: be patient and await his destruction. "Hatta hin" (until a time) means: until a time. They did not specify it; rather, they meant: until a time when fate relieves you of him.

Then Noah (peace be upon him) prayed against his people when he despaired of them. Although his supplication in this verse is not explicit, it is apparent from his saying "for they have denied me," which requires seeking punishment. As for mere support, it would have been achieved by their returning to faith.

Abu Ja'far and Ibn Muhaysin recited "Rabbi unsurni" with a damma on the ba' (ـ "Rabbu"), and likewise "Rabbi uhkum" and similar.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 23, verses 27–30:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿So We revealed to him: "Build the ark under Our eyes and Our revelation. When Our command comes and the oven boils over, then load into it of every kind two mates, and your family, except those against whom the word has already gone forth among them. And do not plead with Me concerning those who have done wrong; indeed they are to be drowned."﴾ ﴿So when you and those with you are settled upon the ark, say: "All praise is for Allah, who has delivered us from the wrongdoing people."﴾ ﴿And say: "My Lord, cause me to land at a blessed landing place, and You are the best of those who bring to land."﴾ ﴿Indeed in that are signs, and indeed We were ever testing.﴾

The discussion of the description and measure of the ship has already preceded in Surah Hud, and "al-Fulk" here is singular, not plural.

His saying, the Exalted: "under Our eyes" is an expression for perception; this is the view of the skilled scholars (al-huddhaq). The Sharia has been established with "a'yun" (plural) and "ayn" (singular), but it is not permissible to say "ʿaynān" (dual), since the Sharia has not been established with the dual form. "Wahyinā" (and Our revelation) means: concerning the manner of the work and the method of its construction. That is because Jibril (peace be upon him) descended to Nuh (peace be upon him) and said to him: "Make such-and-such" for the entire structure of the ship and what it requires. The disbelievers concealed Nuh, because of his claim to prophethood, considering it a mere claim, and they mocked him for building the ship on dry ground, or because it was the first ship, if that is correct.

His saying, the Exalted: "Amrunā" (Our command) may be a verbal noun meaning that We command the water to gush forth, and it may refer to one of the matters, i.e., Our destruction of the disbelievers. The discussion of the meaning of His saying, "and the oven boiled over," has already preceded. The soundest of the views is that it is the oven of bread, and that it was a sign between Allah, Blessed and Exalted, and Nuh (peace be upon him).

His saying, the Exalted: "fasluk" (load) means "fa-adkhil" (enter), and from it is the saying of the poet:

﴿Until they entered the hide, from them, in a musk of the offspring of the she-camel that wanders the horizons, of the bright-skinned kind.﴾

And the saying of another:

﴿And I was a defender of your opponent, I did not flee, while they had pushed you (aslakūka) into a grievous day.﴾

It is said: "salaka" and "aslaka" have the same meaning.

Ḥafṣ, from ʿĀṣim, read "min kullin" with tanwīn on "kullin," while the rest of the readers, and Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim, read it with the idafa "kulli" without tanwīn. And "al-zawjān" is everything whose nature is to be paired from every thing, such as the male and female of animals, and like shoes and others, each one being a mate to the other. This is the position of the word in the language. The arithmeticians apply "zawj" to two, and on this the common usage of the people has settled.

His saying, the Exalted: "wa-ahlaka" (and your family) means his relatives. Then He excepted the one against whom the word had gone forth, namely that he is a disbeliever, and he was his son and his wife. Then Allah commanded Nuh (peace be upon him) not to request of his Lord, nor to address Him interceding for anyone among the wrongdoers. The reference is to those excepted, since it is customary among humans to be tender toward family. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 23, verses 31–34:

The words of the Most High:

﴿Then We brought into being after them another generation.﴾ ﴿And We sent among them a messenger from among themselves, [saying]: "Worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. Will you not then be wary [of Him]?"﴾ ﴿And the chiefs of his people who disbelieved and denied the meeting of the Hereafter, and whom We had given comfort in the life of this world, said: "This is none but a human being like you. He eats of what you eat and drinks of what you drink."﴾ ﴿And if you obey a human being like yourselves, then indeed you would be losers.﴾

al-Tabari (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This generation is Thamud, and their messenger is Salih (peace be upon him). The narrations do imply that the people of 'Ad were earlier, except that they were not destroyed by a blast (sayha). There are many possibilities in this, and Allah knows best.

"Atrafnahum" means: We gave them ease and spread out for them hopes and provisions. The statement of these people also implies their denial of the sending of a human messenger. As for this group and the people of Nuh, these verses do not mention that the miracle appeared to them and that they denied after its clarity. But that is decreed and known, even if the miracle is not specified for us. Punishment does not attach to anyone except after his abandoning what is obligatory upon him, and the obligation of following is only established through the proof (qiyam al-hujjah) being upon the person, or upon the one who is the target and the majority, like the Arabs regarding the miracle of the Qur'an, the physicians regarding 'Isa, and the magicians regarding Musa. Thus, when the proof was established upon these, it was established upon all who came after them.

Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary on Surah 23, verses 35–39:

God Most High says:

﴿Does he promise you that when you die and have become dust and bones, you will indeed be brought forth?﴾ ﴿Far, far is what you are promised!﴾ ﴿There is only our life of this world: we die and we live, and we will not be raised.﴾ ﴿He is only a man who has invented a lie against God, and we will not believe him.﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord, help me, because they have denied me."﴾

His saying, "Does he promise you" (ayya'idukum), is an interrogative (istifham) with the meaning of reproach (tawqif), in the manner of disbelieving it as improbable, and with the meaning of mockery of this promise. The second "annakum" is a substitute (badal) for the first according to Sibawayh, and in it there is the meaning of emphasising the first. It was repeated because of the length of the speech. Al-Mubarrad, however, rejected the expression "substitute," because it is not independent, since it does not mention the predicate (khabar) of the first "anna." According to Sibawayh, the predicate is omitted, and its implied form is: "that you will be resurrected when you die." This implied element is the governing element (al-'amil) of "idha" (when). In the reading of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him, it is: "Does he promise you, when you die and have become dust and bones, that you will indeed be brought forth," with the first "annakum" omitted. By "bringing forth" they mean the resurrection from the graves.

Their saying, "Far, far" (hayhata hayhata), is an expression of improbability. This is a word that carries the meaning of a verb, the implied sense being "far is such-and-such." Sometimes the agent follows it without a lam, as when you say "hayhata majii'a Zayd," meaning "that has become far, the coming of Zayd." From this is the verse of Jarir:

"Far, far is al-'Aqiq and whoever is in it,
and far is a friend with whom we would connect at al-'Aqiq."

Sometimes the agent is omitted, and that is when there is a lam, as in this verse, and the implied sense is: "far is the existence of what you are promised." Because this word has the meaning of a verb, it resembles particles such as "mah" and others, and for that reason it is built (mabni) on fatha. This is the reading of the majority, with a fatha on the ta'. It is a singular noun that was used as a name for the verb in the predicate position, meaning "it has become far," just as "shattan" is a noun meaning "it has separated." The custom of naming a verb in this way is found in the imperative, like "sah" and "hus."

Abu Ja'far read "hayhati hayhati" with a kasra on the ta' and without tanwin. 'Isa ibn 'Umar and Abu Haywa (in one of the transmissions from him) read "hayhata hayhata" with tanwin. According to Sibawayh, in these two readings it is a plural of "hayhat." Its proper form should have been "hayhat," but its weakness did not require the yā' to appear. Sibawayh, may God have mercy on him, said: it is like "bayḍat" (eggs), meaning in that it is a plural. Some grammarians thought that he meant it is like the agreement of a singular form, and they said: the singular of "hayhat" is "hayhih," but that is not what he said. The tanwin in 'Isa's reading is for the sense of indefiniteness, and Abu Ja'far left out the tanwin for the sense of definiteness. 'Isa al-Hamdani read "hayhat hayhat" with a sukun on the ta', and in this case it is a plural, not a singular. Al-A'raj also read it this way, and it is transmitted from Abu 'Amr. Abu Haywa read "hayhatun" with a raised ta' and tanwin, on the basis that it is an independent, declinable (mu'rab) noun whose predicate is ﴿for what you are promised﴾, meaning: the remoteness is for your promise, just as you say: "the star is for your striving." It is also transmitted from Abu Haywa "hayhatu" with damma and without tanwin. Khalid ibn Ilyas read "hayhata hayhata" with fatha and tanwin.

Stopping on "hayhat" depends on the fact that it is built with the ha'. Whoever reads with a kasra on the ta' pauses on the ta'. There are several dialectal forms of the word: "hayha," "hayhat," "hayhan," "ayhat," "hayhat," "hayhat," and "hayhah." Ru'ba said:

"Hayhah from one who tears apart, his hayha'."

Ibn Abi 'Abla read: "hayhata hayhata ma tu'adun" without the lam.

Their saying, ﴿There is only our life of this world﴾, they meant that there is no existence for us other than this existence, and that some of us die and go, and a new group comes. This is the disbelief of the Dahriyya (materialists who deny an afterlife). "Believers" (bi-mu'minin) means "those who affirm." Then their prophet invoked God against them and asked for their punishment because of their denial.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 23, verses 40–44:

The words of the Exalted:

﴿He said, "In a little while they will surely become regretful."﴾ ﴿So the Cry seized them in truth, and We made them debris (ghutha'), so away with the wrongdoing people!﴾ ﴿Then We brought into being after them other generations.﴾ ﴿No nation precedes its term, nor do they delay.﴾ ﴿Then We sent Our messengers in succession (tatra). Every time a messenger came to a nation, they denied him, so We caused them to follow one another, and We made them into tales. So away with a people who do not believe!﴾

The meaning: Allah the Exalted said to this Prophet, the caller: "In a little while your people will regret their disbelief, at a time when regret will not benefit them." Regarding the mention of the Cry, al-Tabari held that they were the people of Thamud. His saying "in truth" means: in accordance with what they deserved from their deeds, and with what was due from Us in their punishment. "Ghutha'" is what the flood carries of its foam and refuse, which is of no benefit; thus every dried-up and perished thing is likened to it. "Bu'dan" (away) is in the accusative by a verb understood and omitted from being expressed.

Then the Exalted informed that He brought into being, after these, many nations, each nation with a term, and in a Book, not exceeding it in its existence or at its death.

"Tatra" is a verbal noun (masdar) in the pattern of fa'la, like da'wa and 'adwa and the like; "tatra" is not a verb, but is a masdar from tawatara al-shay' (a thing came in succession). The majority of readers recited "tatra" as above, pausing on it with an alif. Hamza and al-Kisa'i imala it (pronounced it with inclination toward i). Abu Hatim said: it is the alif of feminine marking. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited "tatraa" with tanwin, and they paused on it with an alif, and it is the alif of extension (ilhaq). Ibn Sida said: it is said, "They came tatra and tatra," meaning successively; the taa' is substituted from the waw without analogical basis, because the analogy for substituting waw with taa' applies only in the pattern if'tala and its derivatives when its first radical is waw, where the waw becomes taa' and is assimilated into the taa' of if'tala, as in "ittazara" and "ittajaha".

As for the Exalted's saying: ﴿So We caused them to follow one another﴾, meaning in destruction. And His saying: ﴿and We made them into tales﴾ intends tales of warning (mathal), and making something into a tale is rarely used except in regard to evil.

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Then We sent Musa and his brother Harun with Our signs and a manifest authority﴾ ﴿to Pharaoh and his chiefs. "Istakbaru" (they behaved arrogantly) means: they refused to believe in Musa and his brother, peace be upon them both, because they were disdainful of that. His saying: ﴿among those destroyed﴾ means: by drowning.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 23, verses 49–51:

The words of the Most High:

﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book, that they might be guided.﴾ ﴿And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign, and We sheltered them on a height, a place of settlement and of flowing water.﴾ ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds. Indeed, I am Knowing of what you do.﴾

"Al-Kitab" (the Book) is the Torah. "La'allahum" (that they might) refers to the Children of Israel, because the Torah was revealed only after the destruction of Pharaoh and the Copts. The expectation (al-taraji) in "la'alla" lies within the domain of human beings, meaning that from Our part there was done with them what leads a son of Adam to hope for their faith and guidance, while the decree has issued what it has issued.

"Ibn Maryam" (the son of Mary) is 'Isa (Jesus), upon him be peace. His story and that of his mother together constitute a great sign as a whole, and there are also signs in its details, and taking it in either of the two senses is valid. "Awa" means "to take in" (damma), and the use of the word for places means: We settled them. "Al-Rabwa" is the elevated part of the land. Most readers recite "rabwatin," while 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir recite it with a fatha (rabwatin), which is also the reading of al-Hasan and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman. Ibn 'Abbas and Nasr, on the authority of 'Asim, recite it with a kasra (ribwatin). Muhammad ibn Ishaq recites "ruba'atin" with a damma on the ra', al-Shuhub al-'Uqayli recites it with a fatha, a group recites it with a kasra, and all of these are dialectal forms in which it was recited. "Al-qarar" means settled stability, so the meaning is that it is level and flat, suitable for tillage and planting, as Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said. Qatada said: "al-qarar" here means grains and fruits.

The meaning of the verse is that it is among the lands whose qualities are complete, so it is fit for one to settle in. It is possible to settle in complete comfort in lands whose water comes from wells, but then He explains that the water of this height is seen flowing visibly on the face of the earth, as Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said, and this is the perfection of perfections.

"Al-ma'in" (flowing water) is that which is apparent in its flowing like a spring, so the mim is augmentative (zā'ida), and it is what one sees flowing, unlike a well and the like. Likewise al-Khalil (ibn Ahmad) placed this word under the root ('ayn, ya', nun). It may also be from their saying "ma'una al-ma'u" (the water became abundant) when it became plentiful, and from it their saying "al-ma'nu al-ma'ruf" (the known generosity) and "al-jud" (liberality). In this case the mim is the first radical of the verb. Al-Tabari cited in support of this the verse of 'Ubayd ibn al-Abras:

"Wahiyatun aw mu'inun mum'inun, wa hadabatun duna-ha luhub" (A ruin, or a spring flowing copiously, and a hill before it with rough ground).

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "May Allah have mercy on Hajar. Had she left Zamzam, it would have been a flowing spring (ʿaynan muʿayyanan)." This can bear both meanings.

This height is the place to which Mary fled when she was in seclusion (istahyat) in the story of 'Isa, upon him be peace, and it is the place in which she was told: ﴿Your Lord has placed a stream beneath you﴾ [Maryam: 24]. This is the view of some of the exegetes.

People differed concerning the location of the height. Ibn al-Musayyib Sa'id said: it is al-Ghouta in Damascus, and this is the most well-known view, because the characteristic of al-Ghouta is that it has a settled stability and flowing water in perfection. Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it is al-Ramla in Palestine, and al-Tabari traced it back to Kurayb, from Murra al-Bahzi, from the Prophet (ﷺ). This view is contradicted by the fact that al-Ramla has absolutely no flowing water. Al-Tabari mentioned it but weakened this view. Ka'b al-Ahbar said: the height is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), and he claimed that the Torah states that Bayt al-Maqdis is the closest of the earth to heaven, and that it rises above the highest part of the earth by eighteen miles.

The qadi Abu Muhammad (Ibn 'Atiyya), may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is more probable that the height is in Bayt Lahm (Bethlehem), which is near Bayt al-Maqdis, because the birth of 'Isa took place there, and the sheltering (al-iwa') then was there.

Abu Zayd said: the height is in the land of Egypt, because it consists of hills to which the flood of the Nile flows, filling the land, while it does not reach those hills, and in them are villages, and in them is their salvation.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This view is weakened by the fact that it has not been related that 'Isa, upon him be peace, and Mary were in the land of Egypt, nor has a story about them there been preserved.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O messengers﴾ may mean: "And We said, O messengers," so this would be one of the stories that He mentioned. Whatever the sense of the statement, they were never addressed all together; rather each one was addressed in his own age. A group recited the address with the words ﴿O messengers﴾ as addressed to Muhammad (ﷺ), and then they differed. Some of them said: he was placed in the position of the messengers, as in His saying: ﴿those to whom the people said, "Indeed the people have gathered against you, so fear them"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 173]. Other things have been said which do not hold up upon reflection. The more correct view in this is that the address is to Muhammad (ﷺ), and this form was used so as to convey concisely that this statement has been addressed to every prophet, or that it is the path which they should follow. This is like when you say to a merchant: "O merchants, you should avoid usury," where you address him in terms of the general meaning, with the addition that this statement is suitable for his entire class. Al-Tabari said: the address in His words, exalted is He, ﴿O messengers﴾ is to 'Isa, upon him be peace. It has been reported that he used to eat from his mother's spinning, but the well-known report is that he used to eat from the herbs of the wilderness. The reason for addressing 'Isa, upon him be peace, is the same as what we mentioned about the assumption that it is addressed to Muhammad (ﷺ).

"Al-tayyibat" (the good things) here means what is lawful with pleasure and otherwise.

In His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, I am Knowing of what you do﴾ there is an admonition to be watchful, and a kind of warning of reckoning, may Allah send blessings upon all His prophets and messengers. If this is the case with them, then what must be the expectation of all people regarding themselves?

Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it is al-Ramla in Palestine, and al-Tabari traced it back to Kurayb, from Murra al-Bahzi, from the Prophet (ﷺ). This view is contradicted by the fact that al-Ramla has absolutely no flowing water. Al-Tabari mentioned it but weakened this view. Ka'b al-Ahbar said: the height is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), and he claimed that the Torah states that Bayt al-Maqdis is the closest of the earth to heaven, and that it rises above the highest part of the earth by eighteen miles.

The qadi Abu Muhammad (Ibn 'Atiyya), may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is more probable that the height is in Bayt Lahm (Bethlehem), which is near Bayt al-Maqdis, because the birth of 'Isa took place there, and the sheltering (al-iwa') then was there.

Abu Zayd said: the height is in the land of Egypt, because it consists of hills to which the flood of the Nile flows, filling the land, while it does not reach those hills, and in them are villages, and in them is their salvation.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This view is weakened by the fact that it has not been related that 'Isa, upon him be peace, and Mary were in the land of Egypt, nor has a story about them there been preserved.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O messengers﴾ may mean: "And We said, O messengers," so this would be one of the stories that He mentioned. Whatever the sense of the statement, they were never addressed all together; rather each one was addressed in his own age. A group recited the address with the words ﴿O messengers﴾ as addressed to Muhammad (ﷺ), and then they differed. Some of them said: he was placed in the position of the messengers, as in His saying: ﴿those to whom the people said, "Indeed the people have gathered against you, so fear them"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 173]. Other things have been said which do not hold up upon reflection. The more correct view in this is that the address is to Muhammad (ﷺ), and this form was used so as to convey concisely that this statement has been addressed to every prophet, or that it is the path which they should follow. This is like when you say to a merchant: "O merchants, you should avoid usury," where you address him in terms of the general meaning, with the addition that this statement is suitable for his entire class. Al-Tabari said: the address in His words, exalted is He, ﴿O messengers﴾ is to 'Isa, upon him be peace. It has been reported that he used to eat from his mother's spinning, but the well-known report is that he used to eat from the herbs of the wilderness. The reason for addressing 'Isa, upon him be peace, is the same as what we mentioned about the assumption that it is addressed to Muhammad (ﷺ).

"Al-tayyibat" (the good things) here means what is lawful with pleasure and otherwise.

In His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, I am Knowing of what you do﴾ there is an admonition to be watchful, and a kind of warning of reckoning, may Allah send blessings upon all His prophets and messengers. If this is the case with them, then what must be the expectation of all people regarding themselves?

Then they divided their affair among themselves into sects, each faction rejoicing in what it has. [23:53]

So leave them in their confusion for a time. [23:54]

Do they think that what We extend to them of wealth and children [23:55] is us hastening good things for them? Rather, they do not perceive. [23:56]

As for the fatḥa on the alif with a shadda on the nūn, the view of Sībawayh is that it is connected at the end to ﴿فاتَّقُونِ﴾ (so fear Me), with the implied meaning "because" (*li-anna*). That is, "so fear Me, because your community is one community and I am your Lord." Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim and Abū ʿAmr read ﴿أُمَّةً واحِدَةً﴾ in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*). It has also been said that it is a substitute for ﴿هَذِهِ﴾, but there is room for consideration in this.

This verse comes after that, with the implied meaning: "And We said to the people." If ﴿يا أيُّها الرُسُلُ﴾ is considered an address to Muhammad (ﷺ), the connection between this and the words ﴿فَتَقَطَّعُوا أمْرَهُمْ﴾ becomes strained. However, although the words ﴿وَأنا رَبُّكم فاتَّقُونِ﴾ (and I am your Lord, so fear Me) were spoken to the prophets, their communities are included in meaning, so the connection of ﴿فَتَقَطَّعُوا﴾ becomes good after that. It is not a reflexive verb (*muṭāwiʿ*) as in when you say "the cloth was cut" (*taqaṭṭaʿa*); rather, it is a transitive verb with the meaning of "they cut" (*qaṭaʿū*). Similar to it are "the night makes me frown" (*tujahhimunī al-layl*), "the journey frightens me" (*tukhawwifunī al-sayr*), and "time makes me aware" (*tuʿarrifunī al-zaman*).

Nāfiʿ reads ﴿زُبُرًا﴾ with a ḍamma on the zāy and the bāʾ, as the plural of *zabūr*. al-Aʿmash and Abū ʿAmr (according to one report) read ﴿زُبُرًا﴾ with a ḍamma on the zāy and a fatḥa on the bāʾ. One is that the communities disputed their affair as revealed books: one faction followed the scrolls, another the Torah, and another the Gospel; then all of them altered and changed them. As for the second reading, its meaning is "divided parties," like *zubar al-ḥadīd* (fragments of iron).

In this verse there is a truce (*muwādaʿa*) that has been abrogated (*mansūkha*) by the verse of the sword.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 23, verses 57–61:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Indeed, those who are, out of fear of their Lord, apprehensive,﴾ ﴿and those who believe in the signs of their Lord,﴾ ﴿and those who do not associate anything with their Lord,﴾ ﴿and those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful that they will return to their Lord.﴾ ﴿It is those who hasten to the good deeds, and they are foremost in them.﴾

When the mention of the disbelievers and their threat was concluded, He followed it with the mention of the believers and their promise, and He mentioned them with their most eloquent attributes. Al-ishfaq (apprehension) is the most intense form of expectation and fear. The "min" in His saying ﴿min khashyati﴾ (out of fear) indicates the kind of apprehension, and apprehension is only of the punishment of Allah, exalted is He. The "min" in our saying "min 'adhabi Allah" (of the punishment of Allah) is for the starting point of a limit (ibtida' ghayah).

The "ayah" (sign) includes the Qur'an, includes lessons (ibar), created things belonging to Allah, the Exalted, and other things in which there is reflection and consideration.

"And in everything there is a sign for Him."

(p-303) Then He mentioned them from the other side, which is the negation of associating partners, because the disbelievers of Quraysh could say: "We too believe in the signs of our Lord," and they wish to affirm that He is the Originator, the Creator. So He mentioned the negation of association, in which they have no share, on account of their idols.

As for His saying ﴿those who give what they give﴾ (wa-alladhina yu'tuna ma ataw): according to the reading of the majority, its meaning is: they give what they have given. Al-Tabari said: he means obligatory zakat and the rest of charity. Something similar is related from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, and Mujahid.

The author, Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What led them to this specification is that "ata'" (giving) is used predominantly for wealth. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr said: it is general over all acts of righteousness, and this is better. It is as if He said: those who give of themselves in obedience to Allah whatever their effort reaches.

'A'ishah, the Mother of the Believers, and Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, and al-A'mash read: ﴿ya'tuna ma ataw﴾ (they do what they did), and its meaning is: they do what they did. This reading is related from the Prophet (ﷺ). One group held that its meaning is: [they abstain] from (p-304) sins. Another group held that this applies to all deeds, obedient and disobedient, and this is the more laudable. Al-Tabari transmitted with a chain from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that she said: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, regarding His saying ﴿those who give what they give﴾ — is it the one who commits adultery and steals?" He said: "No, O daughter of Abu Bakr, rather it is about the man who fasts and gives charity while his heart is fearful, afraid that it will not be accepted from him."

(p-305) The author, Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

There is no room for consideration in the face of the hadith.

Al-wajal (fearfulness) is close in meaning to ishfaq and khawf, and this is the form of that fearfulness. As for the one who mixes good with bad, he should always be under fear that the threat may be carried out against him because of his mixing. Al-Hasan said: its meaning is: those who do what they do of righteousness and fear that this will not save them from the punishment of their Lord.

The author, Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a good expression.

It is also related from al-Hasan that he said: "The believer combines good deeds and compassion, while the hypocrite combines wrongdoing and security."

Al-A'mash read ﴿innahum﴾ with a kasra, as a separate statement containing an implicit warning.

(p-306)

(p-307)

The Most High said: ﴿And We do not burden any soul beyond its capacity, and with Us is a Book that speaks with truth, and they will not be wronged.﴾ ﴿Rather, their hearts are in confusion about this, and they have deeds other than that which they are doing.﴾ ﴿Until when We seize their affluent ones with punishment, behold, they cry out for help.﴾

The Most High's words: ﴿And We do not burden any soul beyond its capacity﴾ abrogate (naskh) everything in the Law that prescribes what is truly beyond human capacity. The imposition of what is beyond capacity (taklif ma la yutaq, the imposition of what cannot be borne) has four types: three are literal, and a fourth is figurative. The figurative type is that which cannot be borne in the sense that one cannot occupy oneself with anything else, such as requiring belief from the disbeliever or obedience from the disobedient. This kind of obligation remains, and it is the obligation of most of the Law. As for the three literal types, two of them occurred in the revelation, and in them abrogation took place: the case of Abu Lahab, which is rationally impossible, and what is customarily impossible in His words: ﴿And whether you reveal what is in yourselves or conceal it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 284], and so on. The third type has nothing revealed about it, and it is the destructive type, because God the Most High did not impose it on His servants. As for the killing of the murderer and the stoning of the adulterer, their punishment is for what they did. The discussion of the question of imposing what is beyond capacity has already been covered comprehensively in the commentary on Surat al-Baqarah. Our saying "abrogating" (nasikh) is open to examination in terms of chronology and what was revealed in Medina and what was revealed in Mecca. And God is the Helper.

The Most High's words: ﴿And with Us is a Book that speaks with truth﴾: the most apparent view about it is that He meant the Book of recording deeds, which the angels raise. On this interpretation, the verse contains a warning and reassurance against injustice and wrongdoing. Another group said that the reference in His words ﴿And with Us is a Book﴾ is to the Qur'an.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is possible, but the first is more apparent.

The Most High's words: ﴿in confusion﴾ mean: in error that has overwhelmed them, as a flooding torrent (ghamr) overwhelms what is in it. His words, glorified be He: "about this" may refer to the Qur'an, or to the Book of recording, or to the righteous deeds mentioned before, meaning: they are in confusion about abandoning and neglecting them. It may also refer to the religion as a whole, or to Muhammad (ﷺ). Each of these interpretations was stated by a group.

The Most High's words: ﴿and they have deeds other than that﴾: the reference by "that" is to the confusion and error encompassing them. So the meaning of the verse is: rather, they are astray, turning away from the truth, and along with that they have schemes of corruption. Thus He characterized them by two evil conditions. Qatada and Abu al-'Aliyah said this meaning. On this interpretation, the statement is about what has already passed of their deeds and what they are engaged in. Another group said the reference by "that" is to His words, glorified be He, "about this," so it is as if He said: they have deeds other than the truth, or the Qur'an and the like. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and Mujahid said: God, glorified and exalted be He, by His words "and they have deeds" informed about what they will undertake of their deeds, meaning: they have deeds of corruption which they will practice.

"Hatta" (until) is purely a particle of beginning, and the first "idha" (when) and the second "idha," which is the answer, prevent it from being a limit (ghayah) for "they are doing."

"Al-mutraf" is the one who is pampered in this world, who has become extravagant (sarf) through it. This condition is common among the leaders of disbelievers in every nation.

"Yajarun" means: they cry out for help with a shriek like the lowing of cattle. The use of al-ja'r (crying out) for humans became frequent, and from it is the verse of al-A'sha:

"He alternates between the prayers of the angel, at one time prostrating, and at another time wailing."

Mujahid and others held that this punishment mentioned is the threat of the day of Badr, and in it there is a criticism of their affluent ones. The pronoun in His words "behold, they" refers only to "the affluent," because they shouted when defeat and slaughter befell them on the day of Badr. It may also refer to the rest after those who were punished. Al-Tabari reported this from Ibn Jurayj, who said: "The ones punished are the slain of Badr, and those who cry out for help are the people of Mecca, because they wailed and sought help."

﴿Do not cry out today; indeed, you will not be helped by Us.﴾ ﴿My verses were recited to you, but you turned back on your heels,﴾ ﴿scornfully, talking nonsense about it at night.﴾ ﴿Have they not pondered the word, or has there come to them what did not come to their forefathers of old?﴾

The meaning: It will be said to them on the Day of punishment, when it descends: ﴿Do not cry out today; indeed, you will not be helped by Us.﴾ This statement may be taken literally, meaning that the angels will say it to them. It may also be taken figuratively, meaning that the tongue of the situation says it. This is on the view that those who cry out are the ones being punished. As for the view of Ibn Jurayj, the angels cannot be the speakers.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿My verses were recited to you﴾ (the verse), refers to the Qur'an. "Tankiṣūn" means that you turn back behind you. This is a metaphor for turning away from and retreating from the truth. 'Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib (may Allah be pleased with him) read: "ʿalā adbārikum tankiṣūn," with a ḍamma on the kāf and with "adbār" (backs) in place of "aʿqāb" (heels). "Mustakbirīn" is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative, describing the state of the subject). The pronoun in "bihi" — the majority said it refers to the Ḥaram (the Sacred Precinct) and the Masjid (the Mosque), even though it has no prior mention, because it was well known in the matter. The meaning is that you believe about yourselves that you have the greatest rights over people through the Masjid and the Ḥaram, and the highest standing with Allah, so you are arrogant because of that, and arrogance is not due to the truth. Another group said the pronoun in "bihi" refers to the Qur'an, from the context in which the verses were mentioned. The meaning is: hearing the verses produces for you disbelief and rebellion.

The author Abū Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This is a good view.

Mundhir ibn Saʿīd mentioned that the pronoun refers to Muḥammad (ﷺ), and it is connected to what follows, as if the speech was complete at "mustakbirīn," and then He said to Muḥammad (ﷺ): ﴿samaran tahjurūn﴾.

(p-309) His saying "samaran" is a ḥāl. It is singular in form but has the meaning of plural. It is said: "qawm samar," "samar," and "sāmir," and its meaning is to stay awake at night. It is derived from "al-samar," which is the shadow cast on figures by the light of the moon. The Arabs used to sit for conversation at night (samar), and this made them knowledgeable about the stars, because they sat in the desert and saw the rising stars from the setting ones. The majority read "sāmiran." Abū Rajā' read "summāran" (plural of sāmir). Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) and ʿIkrima and Ibn Muḥaysin read "samaran," the form that means a night conversation. From this word is the poet's saying:

"Beyond them, if you come upon them at night, [you will find] the strumming of singing-girls and a lavish gathering."

Quraysh used to hold nightly gatherings around the Kaʿba for their falsehoods and their disbelief. The majority read "tahjurūn" with a fatḥa on the tāʾ and a ḍamma on the jīm. The commentators differed on its meaning. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 23, verses 69–71:

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says:

﴿Or do they not recognise their Messenger, so that they deny him?﴾ ﴿Or do they say, "He has a jinn in him"? Nay, he has brought them the truth, but most of them are averse to the truth.﴾ ﴿And if the truth had followed their desires, the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them would have been corrupted. Nay, We have brought them their reminder, but from their reminder they turn away.﴾

This is also a rebuke. The meaning is: did they not know him to be truthful throughout his lifetime, and was there never any denial from them of knowing the person of Muhammad (ﷺ)? Rather, they denied his truthfulness.

As for His saying, ﴿Or do they say, "He has a jinn in him"?﴾, it is also a rebuke, because the difference between wisdom and decisive speech, which he brought, and one who is possessed by a jinn, is not hidden from anyone of sound disposition. Then Allah the Exalted described his state, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, in his coming with the truth.

As for His saying, ﴿And if the truth had followed their desires﴾, Ibn Jurayj and Abu Salih said: "the truth" is Allah the Exalted.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is not in keeping with the pattern of the verse. Others said: the truth here means the correct and the upright.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is the more fitting reading, on the basis that what is mentioned is prior to what Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), brought. On this reading, the corruption of the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them would follow if it were governed by the desires of these people, because they attributed to Allah partners and offspring. If this were the truth, the exalted attributes would not belong to Allah, the Blessed and Exalted; and if He had no such attributes, He would not have that craftsmanship or power, and that would be the corruption of the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them. As for whoever says that "the truth" in the verse is Allah the Exalted, the word "followed" becomes entangled for him, and it becomes difficult for him to arrange the corruption mentioned in the verse; because the word "following," on both readings, is only a metaphor, meaning that their desires would be preserved and established by the truth. We find that Allah the Exalted has decreed the disbelief of nations and their desires, yet there is no corruption of heavens in that. But the truth itself, which is the correct, if it were in accordance with their desires, every thing would be corrupted. So reflect upon it.

Ibn Wathhab recited: ﴿وَلَوِ اتَّبَعَ﴾ with a ḍammah on the wāw. Abu al-Fath said: the ḍammah on this wāw is rare, and the proper view is to liken it to the wāw of plurality, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿اشْتَرَوُا الضَلالَةَ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16] ("they bought the misguidance").

As for His saying, "bi-dhikrihim" (with their reminder), it may mean: with their admonition and clarification to them, as Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said. Qatadah recited "nudhakkiruhum" with a ḍammah on the nūn, a fatḥah on the dhāl, and a kasrah on the kāf with shaddah. It may also mean: with their honour, and this has been narrated. 'Isa ibn 'Umar and Ibn Abi Ishaq recited "ataytuhum bi-dhikrihim" with a ḍammah on the tā' of the speaker. Ibn Abi Ishaq also recited "bal atayta-hum" addressed to Muhammad (ﷺ). The majority recited "bal ataynahum bi-dhikrihim", meaning "we came to them." It is related from Abu 'Amr "ataynahum" with a long vowel, meaning "we gave them."

The majority recited "bal ataynahum bi-dhikrihim", meaning "we came to them." It is related from Abu 'Amr "ataynahum" with a long vowel, meaning "we gave them."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 23, verses 69–71:

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says:

﴿Or do they not recognise their Messenger, so that they deny him?﴾ ﴿Or do they say, "He has a jinn in him"? Nay, he has brought them the truth, but most of them are averse to the truth.﴾ ﴿And if the truth had followed their desires, the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them would have been corrupted. Nay, We have brought them their reminder, but from their reminder they turn away.﴾

This is also a rebuke. The meaning is: did they not know him to be truthful throughout his lifetime, and was there never any denial from them of knowing the person of Muhammad (ﷺ)? Rather, they denied his truthfulness.

As for His saying, ﴿Or do they say, "He has a jinn in him"?﴾, it is also a rebuke, because the difference between wisdom and decisive speech, which he brought, and one who is possessed by a jinn, is not hidden from anyone of sound disposition. Then Allah the Exalted described his state, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, in his coming with the truth.

As for His saying, ﴿And if the truth had followed their desires﴾, Ibn Jurayj and Abu Salih said: "the truth" is Allah the Exalted.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is not in keeping with the pattern of the verse. Others said: the truth here means the correct and the upright.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is the more fitting reading, on the basis that what is mentioned is prior to what Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), brought. On this reading, the corruption of the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them would follow if it were governed by the desires of these people, because they attributed to Allah partners and offspring. If this were the truth, the exalted attributes would not belong to Allah, the Blessed and Exalted; and if He had no such attributes, He would not have that craftsmanship or power, and that would be the corruption of the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them. As for whoever says that "the truth" in the verse is Allah the Exalted, the word "followed" becomes entangled for him, and it becomes difficult for him to arrange the corruption mentioned in the verse; because the word "following," on both readings, is only a metaphor, meaning that their desires would be preserved and established by the truth. We find that Allah the Exalted has decreed the disbelief of nations and their desires, yet there is no corruption of heavens in that. But the truth itself, which is the correct, if it were in accordance with their desires, every thing would be corrupted. So reflect upon it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 23, verses 72–75:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿Or do you ask them for a payment? But the payment of your Lord is better, and He is the best of providers.﴾ ﴿And indeed you call them to a straight path.﴾ ﴿And indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter are deviating from the path.﴾ ﴿And even if We had mercy on them and removed what afflicts them of harm, they would persist in their transgression, wandering blindly.﴾

This is a rebuke directed at them, as if He said: "Did We ask them for wealth, so that they grew distressed by that and found you burdensome because of it?"

Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read: "kharājan fa-kharāju" (خَراجًا فَخَراجُ). Ibn Kathīr, Nāfi' , Abū 'Amr and 'Āṣim read: "kharajan fa-kharāju" (خَرَجًا فَخَراجُ). Ibn 'Abbās (may Allah be pleased with them both) read: "kharjan fa-kharaja" (خُرْجًا فَخَرَجَ), and it is the wealth that is collected and brought at specified times. Al-Aṣma'ī said: the kharj (خَرْج) is a one-time wage (ju'l), while the kharāj (خَراج) is what recurs at certain times.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This is a distinction in usage; otherwise, the two are synonymous in the language, and "kharājan" has also been read in the story of Dhu'l-Qarnayn.

His saying: ﴿fa-kharāju Rabbika﴾ means His reward. He called it kharāj because it was equivalent to the kharāj in this discourse. It may also be that He means: "the provision of your Lord," and this is supported by His saying: ﴿and He is the best of providers.﴾ "Al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm" (the straight path) is the religion of Islam. "Nākibūn" (ناكِبُونَ) means: deviating and turning away.

Then Allah, may He be exalted, informed about them that if the drought were lifted from them, and Allah bestowed upon them abundance and showed them mercy thereby, they would remain upon their disbelief and persist in their transgression. This verse was revealed during the period when the years of drought and hunger afflicted Quraysh, for which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) supplicated in his saying: "O Allah, (send) seven (years) like the years of Yusuf..." — the hadith.

The commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 23, verses 76–77:

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿Indeed, We seized them with punishment, yet they did not humble themselves before their Lord, nor did they entreat Him.﴾ ﴿Until when We opened upon them a gate of severe punishment, behold, they were in despair therein.﴾

This is information from Allah, Exalted and Majestic, about their arrogance and transgression after the hunger had befallen them. This is the view narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and Ibn Jurayj: that "the punishment" is the hunger and drought that came upon them widely, to the point that they ate hides and what was similar to them, and that "the gate" that was threatened is the day of Badr (p-314). This view is refuted by the fact that the drought which afflicted them occurred only after the battle of Badr. «It is narrated that when the hardship reached them, Abu Sufyan came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "Do you not claim, O Muhammad, that you were sent as a mercy to the worlds?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then you have killed the fathers with the sword and the sons with hunger, and we have eaten the 'alhaz." So the verse was revealed.»

"Istakanu" means they lowered themselves and became humble. It may be derived from al-sukun (stillness), in which case it would have to be "istakanu," and it is explained that the fatha on the kaf was prolonged so that an alif was produced. Morphology indicates that it is from "kana" (to be), and that its pattern is (istaf'ala). According to the first view, its pattern is (iftaʿala). That it derives from "kana" is clearer. The meaning is: they did not seek to be people of obedience to their Lord and servants of good.

It is narrated from al-Hasan, may Allah have mercy on him, that he said: "When people are afflicted with a trial from the side of Satan, it is in fact a blessing. So do not meet Allah's blessing with zealous pride, but meet it with seeking forgiveness, and humble yourselves and entreat Allah." And he recited this verse: ﴿Indeed, We seized them with punishment, yet they did not humble themselves before their Lord, nor did they entreat Him.﴾

As for "the severe punishment," it is either the day of Badr with the swords, as some have said, or a threat of an unspecified punishment. The latter is the correct view, because of what we have mentioned, namely that the hunger came before Badr. It is narrated from Mujahid that the punishment and the severe gate are both entirely the famine of the Quraysh.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is good. The "seizing" was at the beginning of the matter, then the gate was opened when it reached its height, when they were reduced to despair, and Abu Sufyan came.

And "al-mublis" (one in despair): the one upon whom evil has descended, and who has despaired of its removal or of its being replaced by good.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 23, verses 78–83:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿It is He who produced for you hearing and sight and hearts; little is it that you give thanks.﴾ ﴿It is He who multiplied you on the earth, and to Him you will be gathered.﴾ ﴿It is He who gives life and causes death, and His is the alternation of night and day. Will you not then reason?﴾ ﴿Rather, they said the like of what the earlier ones said.﴾ ﴿They said: "When we are dead and have become dust and bones, shall we indeed be resurrected?"﴾ ﴿Indeed, we and our forefathers have been promised this before; this is nothing but the fables of the ancients.﴾

He, may He be exalted, began by enumerating blessings, and in the very act of enumerating them there is an argument, through them, for the magnitude of His power, and that the matter of resurrection is not beyond Him nor too great for Him.

"Anshaʾa" means "invented" (ikhtaraʿa). "As-samʿa" (hearing) is a verbal noun (maṣdar), which is why it is given in the singular. It has been said that it intends the genus. "Al-afʾida" means the hearts, and this is a reference to speech and reason (ʿaql). His saying, "qalīlan" (little), is an adjective qualifying an omitted verbal noun, whose implied sense is: "little thanks is it that you give." A group went to the view that it intends: "Little among you is the one who gives thanks," that is, who believes and gives thanks in the true sense of thanks.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The first is more evident.

"Dhara'a" means "scattered and created." His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿and to Him you will be gathered﴾ contains an omitted noun, that is: "to His judgment and His decree." "Tuḥsharūn" (you will be gathered) refers to the sign of resurrection.

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿and His is the alternation of night and day﴾ means: to Him belongs the power from which that arises. "Al-ikhtilāf" (alternation) here means succession, and the state of their being in alternating succession; it is possible that it means the clear difference.

His saying, may He be exalted, "bal" (rather) is a turning away (iḍrāb), and a denial precedes it, implied, as if he said: "They have no reflection on these signs," or something similar. "Al-awwalūn" (the earlier ones) refers by it to the disbelieving nations such as ʿĀd and Thamūd. His saying, may He be exalted, "lamabʿūthūn" means: "indeed to be restored alive." Their saying, "wa-ābāʾunā" (and our forefathers): if the statement is reported from the Arabs, then their meaning is those who passed before from the world, whom they regarded as fathers by virtue of being of one kind; and if it is reported from the earlier ones, then the matter is consistent for them. "Al-asāṭīr" (fables): it has been said that it is the plural of "uslūra," like "u'jūba" and "a'ājīb," and "uḥdūtha" and "aḥādīth"; and it has been said that it is the plural of a plural, as it is said: "saṭr" and "asṭār" and "asāṭīr."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 23, verses 84–89:

His the Exalted's saying:

﴿Say: "To whom belongs the earth and whoever is in it, if you should know?"﴾ ﴿They will say, "To Allah." Say, "Will you not then remember?"﴾ ﴿Say, "Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Great Throne?"﴾ ﴿They will say, "To Allah." Say, "Will you not then fear Him?"﴾ ﴿Say, "In whose hand is the dominion of all things, and He protects while none can be protected against Him, if you should know?"﴾ ﴿They will say, "To Allah." Say, "Then how are you deluded?"﴾

(p-316) Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet ﷺ to make them affirm these matters, which they cannot but acknowledge. And from acknowledging them it follows that they should believe in their Creator and submit to His law and the message of His Messenger.

All readers recited the first "lillah" (to Allah) without disagreement, and they differed regarding the second and third. Abu 'Amr recited "lillah" as a response according to the wording (lafz), while the rest of the Seven recited "lillah" as a response according to the meaning (ma'na). It is as if he had said in the question: "To whom belongs the seven heavens?" since your saying "To whom is this house?" and your saying "Who is the owner of this house?" are the same in meaning.

Then he made the rebuke progressive according to the clarity of the proof, step by step. He stopped at the earth and whoever is in it and matched it with remembrance (tadhakkur). Then he stopped at the seven heavens and the Throne and matched it with taqwa (God-consciousness/fear), which is more emphatic than remembrance; this is according to the clarity of the proof. In His saying "Will you not then fear Him?" there is a warning (wa'id). Then he stopped at the dominion of all things, and in acknowledging this there is a commitment to everything by which victory in argument is achieved. Thereafter the rebuke came in the utmost eloquence in His saying: "Then how are you deluded?" The meaning of "anna" (how? / from where?) is "how?" and "from where?" In this there is an affirmation of their being deluded, and it is a question about the manner in which they were deluded. The word "sihr" (magic, bewitchment) here is used figuratively for them; it is a comparison of what occurred from them of confusion and placing deeds and sayings in other than their proper places, to what occurs from one who is bewitched, and he expressed it thus. A group said: "tusharun" means "you are prevented," and some transmitters related this as a lexical usage.

Ibn Muhaysin recited "al-'Azim" with a raised mim (al-'Azimu), and "malakut" is a verbal noun in the form of intensification (mubalagha). "Al-ijara" means protection from a person; the meaning is that when Allah the Blessed and Exalted prevents someone, he cannot be overpowered, and when He wills something for someone, there is no preventer for him; and likewise in the rest of His power and what His decree executes. Nothing opposes that or diverts it from its course.

Then he made the rebuke progressive according to the clarity of the proof, step by step. He stopped at the earth and whoever is in it and matched it with remembrance (tadhakkur). Then he stopped at the seven heavens and the Throne and matched it with taqwa (God-consciousness/fear), which is more emphatic than remembrance; this is according to the clarity of the proof. In His saying "Will you not then fear Him?" there is a warning (wa'id). Then he stopped at the dominion of all things, and in acknowledging this there is a commitment to everything by which victory in argument is achieved. Thereafter the rebuke came in the utmost eloquence in His saying: "Then how are you deluded?" The meaning of "anna" (how? / from where?) is "how?" and "from where?" In this there is an affirmation of their being deluded, and it is a question about the manner in which they were deluded. The word "sihr" (magic, bewitchment) here is used figuratively for them; it is a comparison of what occurred from them of confusion and placing deeds and sayings in other than their proper places, to what occurs from one who is bewitched, and he expressed it thus. A group said: "tusharun" means "you are prevented," and some transmitters related this as a lexical usage.

Ibn Muhaysin recited "al-'Azim" with a raised mim (al-'Azimu), and "malakut" is a verbal noun in the form of intensification (mubalagha). "Al-ijara" means protection from a person; the meaning is that when Allah the Blessed and Exalted prevents someone, he cannot be overpowered, and when He wills something for someone, there is no preventer for him; and likewise in the rest of His power and what His decree executes. Nothing opposes that or diverts it from its course.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 23, verses 90–92:

His the Mighty and Majestic's saying:

﴿Rather, We brought them the truth, and indeed they are liars.﴾ ﴿Allah has not taken any son, and there was not with Him any god; for then each god would have gone off with what he created, and some of them would have overpowered others. Glory be to Allah above what they describe.﴾ ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed; so exalted is He above what they associate with Him.﴾

The meaning: The matter is not as they say, attributing to Allah the Exalted what is not befitting for Him. Rather, We brought them [the truth]. Ibn Abi Ishaq read "ataynahum" (آتَيْناهُمْ) in the second person addressed to Muhammad (ﷺ). "Liars" (لَكاذِبُونَ) is meant as: in what they ascribed to Allah the Exalted of companions, sons and partners. In His saying, the Exalted, ﴿and there was not with Him any god﴾, there is evidence of mutual hindrance (al-tamanu', mutual obstruction). This is the corruption that His saying, the Exalted, comprehends: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would have been corrupted﴾ [al-Anbiya': 22]. A created part (al-juz' al-mukhtara') cannot be the object of two powers or more. And if two gods differed in a will, then the execution of both would be impossible and the incapacity of both would be impossible. So when the will of the one stands alone, he is the Exalted, and the other is not a god. If it is said: "We assume that they do not differ in a will," it is answered: that would occur; and when the disbelievers permit it, the proof is established against them, for what is committed to be permissible takes the place, in the argument, of what is committed to be actual.

His the Exalted's saying "idhan" (إذًا) is the answer to an omitted clause, whose estimate is: "Had there been with Him a god, then each god would have gone off." Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs from 'Asim read "'Alimi al-ghayb" (عالَمِ الغَيْبِ) with a kasra on the mim, following the written form in His saying "Subhan Allah." The rest, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim, read "'Alimu al-ghayb" (عالَمُ الغَيْبِ) with a raf' (nominative). The meaning: He is the Knower. Al-Akhfash said: the genitive is better so that the speech is of one aspect. Abu 'Ali said: the reason for the raf' is that the speech has been cut off.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"The inchoative (al-ibtida') is, in my view, more excellent."

The fa' (ف) in His the Exalted's saying "fa-ta'ala" (فَتَعالى) is conjunctive in meaning, as if He said: "The Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, so exalted is He." This is like your saying: "Zayd is brave, so his rank is great," i.e., he was brave, so it became great. It may also be that the meaning is: "So I say, exalted is He above what they associate," as a new independent statement. "Al-ghayb" (الغَيْب) is what is hidden from people, and "al-shahada" (الشَهادَة) is what they have witnessed.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 23, verses 93–98:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Say: "My Lord, if You should show me that which they are promised,﴾ ﴿My Lord, then do not place me among the wrongdoing people."﴾ ﴿And indeed, We are able to show you what We promise them.﴾ ﴿Repel evil by that which is best; We are most knowing of what they describe.﴾ ﴿And say, "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the incitements of the devils."﴾ ﴿And I seek refuge in You, My Lord, lest they be present with me.﴾

Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to supplicate for himself deliverance from the punishment of the wrongdoers, should it have been decreed that he would witness that. "In" (إنْ) is a conditional particle, and "ma" (ما) is an added particle. "Turiyanni" (تُرِيَنِّي) is in the jussive mood because of the conditional, and the heavy nun (النون الثقيلة) is obligatory with it. According to al-Mubarrad, it never separates from "imma" (إمّا). According to Sibawayh, it is permissible for it to be separated, so one says "imma turiyanni", but the usage of the Qur'an is its obligation, and from there al-Mubarrad adopted this position.

This supplication contains the maintenance of apprehension and warning concerning the matter for which they are punished. Then its like for the rest of the community is a supplication for a good end. Within this verse, in its entirety, is an announcement of the nearness of the punishment to them, as it was on the day of Badr. His saying a second time, "My Lord," is an interjection between the condition and its answer.

In His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Repel evil by that which is best﴾, the verse is a command to forgiveness and noble character. Whatever of it pertains to this is a ruling that remains in the community forever. What it contains of the meaning of truce with the disbelievers, leaving off confronting them, and overlooking their affairs, is abrogated by fighting. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We are most knowing of what they describe﴾ requires that it is a verse of truce. Mujahid said: repelling with that which is best is greeting; he greets him when he meets him. Al-Hasan said: By Allah, none attains it until he swallows his rage and forgives what he dislikes.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

These are the two extremes. In this verse there is a promise to the Prophet (ﷺ), meaning: occupy yourself with this, and leave their punishment and retribution to Us. He commanded him to seek refuge from the devil in his incitements, which are the fits of anger in which a person does not control himself. It seems these were what used to strike the believers together with the disbelievers, so hostility occurs; therefore it is connected to this verse. Ibn Zayd said: the incitement (همز) of the devil is madness.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In the Musannaf of Abu Dawud, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O Allah, I seek refuge in You from the devil, his incitement, his blowing, and his spitting." Abu Dawud said: "Its incitement (همزة) is the 'death-stroke', which is madness; its blowing is pride; its spitting is magic."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The promptings (النزغات) and fits of anger are from the devil, and they are what is sought refuge from in the verse. Seeking refuge from madness is also a scheme. In the recitation of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "My Lord, seeking refuge in You from the incitements of the devils, and seeking refuge in You, My Lord, lest they be present." His saying, ﴿lest they be present with me﴾ means: lest they be with me in my affairs, for when they are present with a person they are prepared for incitement, and when there is no presence, there is no incitement.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The root of al-hamz (الهمز) is pushing and jabbing with the hand and other than it; from it come "hamz al-khayl" (pricking horses) and "hamz an-nas bil-lisan" (slandering people with the tongue). It was said to one of the Arabs: "Do you hamz the mouse?" He was asked about the word, so he thought the intended referent was the mouse itself, and said: "The cat hamzes it."

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:
