Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to supplicate for himself deliverance from the punishment of the wrongdoers, should it have been decreed that he would witness that. "In" (إنْ) is a conditional particle, and "ma" (ما) is an added particle. "Turiyanni" (تُرِيَنِّي) is in the jussive mood because of the conditional, and the heavy nun (النون الثقيلة) is obligatory with it. According to al-Mubarrad, it never separates from "imma" (إمّا). According to Sibawayh, it is permissible for it to be separated, so one says "imma turiyanni", but the usage of the Qur'an is its obligation, and from there al-Mubarrad adopted this position.

This supplication contains the maintenance of apprehension and warning concerning the matter for which they are punished. Then its like for the rest of the community is a supplication for a good end. Within this verse, in its entirety, is an announcement of the nearness of the punishment to them, as it was on the day of Badr. His saying a second time, "My Lord," is an interjection between the condition and its answer.

In His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Repel evil by that which is best﴾, the verse is a command to forgiveness and noble character. Whatever of it pertains to this is a ruling that remains in the community forever. What it contains of the meaning of truce with the disbelievers, leaving off confronting them, and overlooking their affairs, is abrogated by fighting. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We are most knowing of what they describe﴾ requires that it is a verse of truce. Mujahid said: repelling with that which is best is greeting; he greets him when he meets him. Al-Hasan said: By Allah, none attains it until he swallows his rage and forgives what he dislikes.

These are the two extremes. In this verse there is a promise to the Prophet (ﷺ), meaning: occupy yourself with this, and leave their punishment and retribution to Us. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 23, verses 99–102:

The words of the Most High:

﴿Until, when death comes to one of them, he says, "My Lord, send me back,﴾ ﴿so that I may do righteous deeds in what I have left behind." No! It is only a word he speaks. Behind them is a barzakh until the Day they are resurrected.﴾ ﴿So when the Trumpet is blown, there will be no kinship between them that day, nor will they ask one another.﴾ ﴿As for him whose scales are heavy, those are the successful.﴾

"Ḥattā" (until) in this place is a *ḥarf ibtidāʾ* (an inceptive particle, introducing a new statement), and it is possible that it is a pure limit (*ghāya mujarrada*) with an omitted clause implied. The first is clearer, because what follows it is the thing intended and meant to be mentioned. The pronoun in "aḥadahum" refers to the disbelievers. His saying "irjiʿūn" (send me back) means: back to the life of this world. The plural pronoun can be explained in two ways: either he addresses [his Lord] in the plural of majesty, in the manner of God Most High speaking of Himself with the plural "we" in more than one place; or it is a plea to his Lord first, and then he addresses the angels of punishment with his words "irjiʿūn." Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it refers to the polytheist. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to ʿĀʾisha (may Allah be pleased with her): "When the believer sees [the angels], the angels say to him: 'Shall we return you?' He says: 'To the abode of worries and sorrows? Rather, forward to Allah, the Exalted.' As for the disbeliever, he says: 'Send me back, so that I may do righteous deeds.'" Al-Ḥasan and the majority read "laʿallī" with a sukūn on the yāʾ, and Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif read (p-321) "laʿallī" with a fatḥa on the yāʾ. "Kallā" is a word of rebuke (*kalimat zajr*), and it is part of the speech of Allah the Most High.

His saying: ﴿It is only a word he speaks﴾ may carry three meanings. The first: a emphatic report that this thing will happen and he will say this word. The second: the meaning is, "It is a word that does not avail him more than his saying it, and there is no benefit or relief for him in it." The third: it is an indication that if he were returned, he would revert [to what he was doing], and so it is a verse of censure against them. The pronoun in "warāʾihim" refers to the disbelievers, meaning that after their death there comes a barrier of time. In the language of the Arabs, *barzakh* is the barrier between two distances, and then it is used metaphorically for anything beyond that. Here it is for the period between a person's death and his resurrection; this is a consensus (*ijmāʿ*) of the exegetes. "Yawm" is in apposition to / governs the phrase "yubʿathūn" (they are resurrected).

The majority read "fī al-ṣūr," meaning the horn. Ibn ʿIyāḍ read "fī al-ṣuwar" with a fatḥa on the wāw, as the plural of ṣūra (form). As for His saying, ﴿So there will be no kinship between them that day﴾, the interpreters differed about the nature of the cancelling of kinship. Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both) and others said: this is at the first blast, because all people die together, so there will be no kinship between them at that time, since they are dead.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This interpretation removes from the verse the mention of the terror of the gathering.

Ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him) and others said: the meaning is rather that at the second blast, when people rise from their graves, they are then occupied with the terror of the standing-place, each person preoccupied with himself. Means of connection have been severed among them, and the benefit of kinship has ceased. Therefore He negates it. So the meaning is: there are no kinships that benefit. It is related from Qatāda that there is no one more hateful to a person on that day than one who knows him, because he fears that he has a wrong (*maẓlama*) against him. On that day a person flees from his brother, his mother, his father, his wife and his sons, and each person on that day rejoices that he has a right against his son or his father. A hadith has been transmitted with this. Likewise, the cessation of questioning is in line with these aspects that we have mentioned; then there come in the Resurrection stations in which there is questioning and recognition.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This interpretation is good, and it is the meaning transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both).

The heaviness of the scales is by good deeds, and heaviness and lightness are only alternately applied to bodies which Allah the Most High creates with that property, and they are, as has been related, certificates (*barāʾāt*).

﴿As for him whose scales are light, those are the ones who have lost their souls; in Hell they will abide forever.﴾ ﴿The Fire will sear their faces, and they will be grim-faced within it.﴾ ﴿Were not My signs recited to you, and did you not deny them?﴾ ﴿They will say: "Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us, and we were a misguided people.﴾ ﴿Our Lord, bring us out of it; then if we return, we will indeed be wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿He will say: "Be gone into it, and do not speak to Me."﴾

The plural "al-mawazin" (the scales), with respect to what is weighed, is plural, and what is weighed is the deeds. The meaning of weighing (al-wazn) is establishing the proof against people through what is perceptible, according to their custom and convention. The weighing of the disbelievers is in one of two ways: either their disbelief is placed in one pan, and they find nothing to balance it in the other pan; or their deeds, such as kinship ties and acts of righteousness, are placed in the pan of good deeds, and then their disbelief is placed in the other pan, so their deeds become light.

"Lafh al-nar" (the Fire's scorching) means its reaching them with heat and burning. Abu Haywa recited "kalihun" (grim-faced) without an alif. "Al-kalah" is the baring of the lips away from the teeth. This happens to a person during a violent confrontation in anger, and it happens to heads in the fire. 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) likened what is in this verse to what happens to the heads of rams when they are singed with fire, for they become grim-faced (takluh). From this comes the baring of the teeth of a dog and a lion (kulul al-kalb wal-asad). The term is also used metaphorically for times and calamities.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Were not My signs recited to you﴾ is preceded by an omitted element, whose implied meaning is: it will be said to them. The "ayat" (signs) here means the Qur'an. He informed us that when they hear this reproach they submit, acknowledge against themselves, and surrender with their saying: ﴿our wretchedness overcame us, and we were a misguided people.﴾ The majority of reciters read "shiqwatuna" with a kasra on the shin and no alif, and this is the reading of the two Haram (Meccan and Medinan) readers. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "shaqawatuna" with a fatha on the shin and an alif after the qaf, and this is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud. 'Asim allowed either of the two readings. Both are verbal nouns from "shaqiya, yashqa" (to be wretched). Then they progressed from acknowledgment to desire and entreaty, because they had become humbled, since acknowledging sin is an excuse and a disclaiming. So the answer to their request came in accordance with what Allah, exalted is He, had decreed of their punishment, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Be gone into it, and do not speak to Me.﴾ The phrase "wa la tukallimun" (and do not speak to Me) came in the form of a prohibition, though they are not able to speak, according to what has been reported. This is an exaggeration in forbidding. It is said that when they hear this word, they despair.

Al-Tabari related a lengthy narration about a dialogue that takes place between the disbelievers and Malik, the keeper of the Fire, and then between them and their Lord. Its final part is this statement, "Be gone into it." He said: then Hell closes over them, despair sets in, and they remain barking at one another's faces.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

I have abridged that narration because it is not authentic, but its meaning is sound. May Allah protect us from His Fire by His grace.

His saying, exalted is He: "Be gone" (ukhsa'u) is a rebuke, and it is used in rebuking dogs. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Ibn Sayyad: "Be gone; you will never exceed your measure."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 23, verses 109–111:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Indeed, there was a group of My servants who said, "Our Lord, we have believed, so forgive us and have mercy upon us, and You are the best of the merciful."﴾ ﴿But you took them in mockery until they made you forget My remembrance, and you used to laugh at them.﴾ ﴿Indeed, I have rewarded them today for their patience; indeed, they are the triumphant.﴾

Harun read "أنَّهُ كانَ" (innahu kana) with an open alif (fatha on the alif), which is the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him. It is also reported that in the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b it is "أنْ كانَ" (an kana). All of this is mutually supporting. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, it is "وَلا تُكَلِّمُونِ كانَ فَرِيقٌ" (wa la tukallimun, kana fariq), without "إنَّهُ" (innahu). This strengthens the kasra on the alif of "إنَّهُ" (innahu), since it is a resumption (isti'naf). This hā' is an ambiguous pronoun referring to the matter (ḍamīr al-amr), which the Kufans call the "unknown" (al-majhūla), and that is an erroneous expression. This entire verse is among those things said to the disbelievers by way of reproach.

The group referred to is every oppressed believer whose situation happens to be like this situation with disbelievers. The verse was revealed concerning the disbelievers of Quraysh together with Suhayb, 'Ammar and Bilal, may Allah be pleased with them all, and their counterparts. Then it is general concerning whoever followed their path in earlier times and for the rest of time.

Nafi', Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "سُخْرِيًّا" (sukhriyyan) with a ḍamma on the sin, and the rest read "سِخْرِيًّا" (sikhriyyan) with a kasra. One group said both have the same meaning, and al-Tabari mentioned this. Abu Zayd al-Ansari said they mean mockery (al-huzw). Abu 'Ubayda and others said that the ḍamma on the sin is from servitude (al-sukhra) and making someone serve (al-takhdim), while the kasra on the sin is from mockery (al-sikhr), which is ridicule (al-istihza'), and from it is the saying of al-A'sha:

؎ Indeed there came to me a report about which I do not keep secret, from on high; there is no lie in it, nor mockery (sukhr).

Abu 'Ali said: the reading with a kasra on the sin is more eloquent, because it means ridicule, and the kasra is more common in it, and it is more fitting to the verse. Do you not see His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and you used to laugh at them﴾?

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Do you not see the consensus of the reciters on the ḍamma on the sin in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿that some of them may take others in service (sukhriyyan)﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 32], since the matter is clearly about making someone serve. Yunus said: when servitude is intended, it is with a ḍamma on the sin only; when mockery is intended, it is with either the ḍamma or the kasra. The companions of 'Abd Allah, al-A'raj and Ibn Abi Ishaq read everything in the Qur'an with a ḍamma on the sin, while al-Hasan and Abu 'Amr read everything in the Qur'an with a kasra except the one in al-Zukhruf, where they both used a ḍamma on the sin, as the people did, since it is from servitude. He attributed the forgetting to the group because it was on account of them, and the meaning is that their occupation with mocking these people made them forget what would benefit them.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read "أنَّهم هُمُ الفائِزُونَ" (annahum humu al-fa'izun) with an open alif, so "جَزَيْتُهُمْ" (jazaytuhum) governs "أنَّ" (anna), and it is permissible that it governs a deleted object, the estimate being: because they. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Kharija from Nafi' read "إنَّهم هُمُ الفائِزُونَ" (innahum humu al-fa'izun) with a kasra on the alif, so the second object of "جَزَيْتُ" (jazayt) is understood, its estimate being: the Garden or the good pleasure. "Al-fa'izun" are those who reach their goal which they had hoped for. The meaning of triumph (al-fawz) is deliverance from ruin to blessing.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 23, verses 109–111:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Indeed, there was a group of My servants who said, "Our Lord, we have believed, so forgive us and have mercy upon us, and You are the best of the merciful."﴾ ﴿But you took them in mockery until they made you forget My remembrance, and you used to laugh at them.﴾ ﴿Indeed, I have rewarded them today for their patience; indeed, they are the triumphant.﴾

Harun read "أنَّهُ كانَ" (innahu kana) with an open alif (fatha on the alif), which is the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him. It is also reported that in the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b it is "أنْ كانَ" (an kana). All of this is mutually supporting. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, it is "وَلا تُكَلِّمُونِ كانَ فَرِيقٌ" (wa la tukallimun, kana fariq), without "إنَّهُ" (innahu). This strengthens the kasra on the alif of "إنَّهُ" (innahu), since it is a resumption (isti'naf). This hā' is an ambiguous pronoun referring to the matter (ḍamīr al-amr), which the Kufans call the "unknown" (al-majhūla), and that is an erroneous expression. This entire verse is among those things said to the disbelievers by way of reproach.

The group referred to is every oppressed believer whose situation happens to be like this situation with disbelievers. The verse was revealed concerning the disbelievers of Quraysh together with Suhayb, 'Ammar and Bilal, may Allah be pleased with them all, and their counterparts. Then it is general concerning whoever followed their path in earlier times and for the rest of time.

Nafi', Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "سُخْرِيًّا" (sukhriyyan) with a ḍamma on the sin, and the rest read "سِخْرِيًّا" (sikhriyyan) with a kasra. One group said both have the same meaning, and al-Tabari mentioned this. Abu Zayd al-Ansari said they mean mockery (al-huzw). Abu 'Ubayda and others said that the ḍamma on the sin is from servitude (al-sukhra) and making someone serve (al-takhdim), while the kasra on the sin is from mockery (al-sikhr), which is ridicule (al-istihza'), and from it is the saying of al-A'sha:

؎ Indeed there came to me a report about which I do not keep secret, from on high; there is no lie in it, nor mockery (sukhr).

Abu 'Ali said: the reading with a kasra on the sin is more eloquent, because it means ridicule, and the kasra is more common in it, and it is more fitting to the verse. Do you not see His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and you used to laugh at them﴾?

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Do you not see the consensus of the reciters on the ḍamma on the sin in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿that some of them may take others in service (sukhriyyan)﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 32], since the matter is clearly about making someone serve. Yunus said: when servitude is intended, it is with a ḍamma on the sin only; when mockery is intended, it is with either the ḍamma or the kasra. The companions of 'Abd Allah, al-A'raj and Ibn Abi Ishaq read everything in the Qur'an with a ḍamma on the sin, while al-Hasan and Abu 'Amr read everything in the Qur'an with a kasra except the one in al-Zukhruf, where they both used a ḍamma on the sin, as the people did, since it is from servitude. He attributed the forgetting to the group because it was on account of them, and the meaning is that their occupation with mocking these people made them forget what would benefit them.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read "أنَّهم هُمُ الفائِزُونَ" (annahum humu al-fa'izun) with an open alif, so "جَزَيْتُهُمْ" (jazaytuhum) governs "أنَّ" (anna), and it is permissible that it governs a deleted object, the estimate being: because they. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Kharija from Nafi' read "إنَّهم هُمُ الفائِزُونَ" (innahum humu al-fa'izun) with a kasra on the alif, so the second object of "جَزَيْتُ" (jazayt) is understood, its estimate being: the Garden or the good pleasure. "Al-fa'izun" are those who reach their goal which they had hoped for. The meaning of triumph (al-fawz) is deliverance from ruin to blessing.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 23, verses 112–115:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿He will say, "How many years did you remain on the earth?"﴾ ﴿They will say, "We remained a day or part of a day; so ask those who count."﴾ ﴿He will say, "You remained only a little, if only you had known."﴾ ﴿Did you think that We created you without purpose, and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾

Nafi', 'Asim, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir recited: "qala kam labithtum" and "qul in labithtum." Al-Bizzi related from Ibn Kathir "qala in labithtum" as a statement (khabar). Abu 'Amr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i assimilated the taa' (idgham), while the rest did not assimilate it. The meaning of the first reading is a report that God enables them to be asked about the duration, then later informs them of their brief stay. The meaning of the second is a command to one of them who is indicated, in the sense: it is said to one of them, "Say such-and-such." When he says something other than what is upright, he is told, "Say: if you remained..." The meaning of al-Bizzi's narration is: a prompting (tawqif) followed by a report. In the mushafs, "qala" appears in both places, except in the Kufan mushaf, which has "qul" without the alif.

As for His saying, "fi al-ard" (on the earth), al-Tabari said: its meaning is: in the world, alive, and it is on this basis that the question was posed, and they forgot because of the intensity of the terror of the punishment, to the point that they said: ﴿a day or part of a day﴾.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The purpose of this is to make them acknowledge that their lives were short, and that their disbelief brought them to a long punishment.

The majority of the interpreters said: in the depths of the earth, dead.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is the more correct view, since they denied resurrection, and their saying was that they would not rise from the dust. It is said to them when they have risen: "How long did you remain?" And His saying at the end: ﴿and that you would not be returned to Us﴾ supports what we have said.

"'Adad" is in the accusative governed by "kam" as a specification (tamyiz). Al-A'mash recited "'adadan sinin," with tanwin on "'adadan."

Mujahid said: by "al-'adDin" (those who count) they meant the angels. Qatada said: they meant the people of reckoning.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The apparent sense of the wording is that they meant those who are characterized by this attribute, and they did not specify angels or others, because a sleeper or a dead person does not count movement, so no time is measured for him.

His saying, ﴿You remained only a little﴾, its aim, on the view that the stay was in the world, is: little in quantity compared with what you were punished. On the view that the stay was in the graves, its meaning is that it is little, since everything that is coming is near, but you denied it because you did not know, for you did not desire knowledge and guidance.

"'Abathan" means: in vain, without an intended end. The majority recited "turja'un" with a dammah on the taa' and a fathah on the jim. Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "turja'un" with a fathah on the taa' and a kasrah on the jim. The meaning in both is clear.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 23, verses 116–118:

Allah, the Exalted, says:

﴿So exalted is Allah, the True King; there is no god except Him, Lord of the Honorable Throne.﴾ ﴿And whoever invokes along with Allah another god, for which he has no proof, then his account is only with his Lord. Indeed, the disbelievers will not succeed.﴾ ﴿And say, "My Lord, forgive and have mercy, and You are the best of the merciful."﴾

The meaning: "So exalted is Allah" above what they say concerning Him regarding companions and offspring, and above their reckoning that they will not return. That is, Allah is far removed from those matters and exalted above them. Ibn Muhaysin read "al-Karīm" (the Honorable) in the nominative as an attribute of "al-Rabb" (the Lord).

Then, may His power be majestic, He threatened the worshippers of idols with His saying, may He be blessed and exalted: ﴿And whoever invokes along with Allah another god﴾, to the end of the verse. The threat is His saying: ﴿then his account is only with his Lord.﴾

"Al-burhān" means the proof. The apparent sense of the speech is that "man" (whoever) is a conditional particle, and its answer is in His saying: ﴿then his account is only with his Lord﴾, while His saying: ﴿for which he has no proof﴾ is in the position of a qualifier. Some people held that the answer is in His saying "for which he has no proof," but this is an evasion from the implication of the discourse, namely that there might be a caller to it who has a proof.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is an unnecessary restriction, and it would entail omitting the fa' (fā') from the answer of the conditional, which is not eloquent, as Sibawayh said. In the reading of 'Abdullah it is "ʿinda rabbika" (with your Lord), and in the reading of Ubayy it is "ʿinda Allāh" (with Allah). It is also narrated that it contains "ʿalā Allāh" (upon Allah). Then He decreed and affirmed that the disbeliever does not attain his wish and his effort does not succeed. Al-Jumhur read "innahu lā yuflihu" with a kasra on the alif, while al-Hasan and Qatada read "annahu" with a fatha on it. The meaning is that, since he is not mentioned and does not prosper, He postpones his reckoning and his punishment until he meets his Lord. Al-Hasan read "yaflaḥu" with a fatha on the ya' and the lam.

(p-328) Then He commanded the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to supplicate for forgiveness and mercy, and to mention Him by declaring that He is the best of the merciful, because every merciful person acts only by the will of Allah, His granting of success, and His decree of the measure of this mercy. His mercy, may He be exalted, has no partner in it for anyone. Also, the mercy of every merciful person is in particular things and by particular means, which are trivial in comparison with the matters in which the mercy of Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, takes place, such as rescue from the Fire and the form of the bliss of Paradise. And according to what is in the hadith, the mercy of every merciful person, all of it together, is a part of one hundredth of the mercy of Allah, the Exalted, may His power be majestic; for He dispersed one part into the world and kept ninety-nine parts with Himself.

Ibn Muhaysin read "wa qul rabbu ighfir" with a damma on the ba' of "rabb".

The commentary on Surah al-Mu'minun is complete, and all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

In the reading of 'Abdullah it is "ʿinda rabbika" (with your Lord), and in the reading of Ubayy it is "ʿinda Allāh" (with Allah). It is also narrated that it contains "ʿalā Allāh" (upon Allah). Then He decreed and affirmed that the disbeliever does not attain his wish and his effort does not succeed. Al-Jumhur read "innahu lā yuflihu" with a kasra on the alif, while al-Hasan and Qatada read "annahu" with a fatha on it. The meaning is that, since he is not mentioned and does not prosper, He postpones his reckoning and his punishment until he meets his Lord. Al-Hasan read "yaflaḥu" with a fatha on the ya' and the lam.

(p-328) Then He commanded the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to supplicate for forgiveness and mercy, and to mention Him by declaring that He is the best of the merciful, because every merciful person acts only by the will of Allah, His granting of success, and His decree of the measure of this mercy. His mercy, may He be exalted, has no partner in it for anyone. Also, the mercy of every merciful person is in particular things and by particular means, which are trivial in comparison with the matters in which the mercy of Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, takes place, such as rescue from the Fire and the form of the bliss of Paradise. And according to what is in the hadith, the mercy of every merciful person, all of it together, is a part of one hundredth of the mercy of Allah, the Exalted, may His power be majestic; for He dispersed one part into the world and kept ninety-nine parts with Himself.

Ibn Muhaysin read "wa qul rabbu ighfir" with a damma on the ba' of "rabb".

The commentary on Surah al-Mu'minun is complete, and all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 23, verses 116–118:

Allah, the Exalted, says:

﴿So exalted is Allah, the True King; there is no god except Him, Lord of the Honorable Throne.﴾ ﴿And whoever invokes along with Allah another god, for which he has no proof, then his account is only with his Lord. Indeed, the disbelievers will not succeed.﴾ ﴿And say, "My Lord, forgive and have mercy, and You are the best of the merciful."﴾

The meaning: "So exalted is Allah" above what they say concerning Him regarding companions and offspring, and above their reckoning that they will not return. That is, Allah is far removed from those matters and exalted above them. Ibn Muhaysin read "al-Karīm" (the Honorable) in the nominative as an attribute of "al-Rabb" (the Lord).

Then, may His power be majestic, He threatened the worshippers of idols with His saying, may He be blessed and exalted: ﴿And whoever invokes along with Allah another god﴾, to the end of the verse. The threat is His saying: ﴿then his account is only with his Lord.﴾

"Al-burhān" means the proof. The apparent sense of the speech is that "man" (whoever) is a conditional particle, and its answer is in His saying: ﴿then his account is only with his Lord﴾, while His saying: ﴿for which he has no proof﴾ is in the position of a qualifier. Some people held that the answer is in His saying "for which he has no proof," but this is an evasion from the implication of the discourse, namely that there might be a caller to it who has a proof.
